script.text: My teacher knew what time my bedroom light went off. I hadn't told him. I hadn't told anyone.
Okay. Let me go back, because that sounds like the end of a horror movie. I was fifteen. This was an ordinary school, with broken fans and a bell that sounded personally offended.
He taught English. Everyone liked him. He remembered birthdays, lent people books, stayed after class. You know, the teacher your parents called dedicated.
At first, he just asked about my drawings. He'd stop beside my desk and say, you're quiet today. And I thought, oh. Somebody actually noticed.
Then he started keeping my notebook after class. Just a minute, he'd say. The minute always lasted until the corridor was empty.
Nothing dramatic happened. That was the confusing part. He'd ask who I walked home with. Whether my mum worked late. Questions that didn't belong anywhere near my English homework.
I answered because he was a teacher. Saying, why do you need to know that, felt ruder than giving him my entire afternoon.
One day he asked why I'd stopped taking the main road home. I laughed. Like, awkward little laugh. Then I realized I hadn't mentioned changing my route.
He said he'd seen me from his car. Perfectly normal explanation. Except the shortcut was behind the shops. You couldn't see it from the main road.
I told my friend. We did that thing where you make something a joke so you don't have to decide how scared you are. Oh, great. Personal attendance service.
She walked home with me the next day. We stopped at a stationery shop. Across the street, beside a parked car, was my teacher.
He didn't wave. Didn't come over. Just looked at us. My friend stopped laughing before I did.
After that, I started noticing the same car. Near the school gate. Outside the bakery. Once, at the end of my lane. I kept inventing reasons for it to be there.
Then a message came from a number I didn't recognize. Did you get home safely? It was him. He said he'd got my number from the school contact list.
I typed, yes sir, thank you. I hate remembering that. I was scared, and I still added thank you.
The messages got stranger. You're up late. Who was that with you? Then, don't mention these chats at school. People misunderstand kindness.
I didn't reply to that one. The next morning he put my notebook on my desk, leaned down, and said, ignoring people isn't very nice.
He said it softly. Everyone else was getting their books out. I remember staring at the date on the board because looking at him felt impossible.
That evening, I left my lamp on while I went downstairs. When I came back, there was another message. Long night studying?
My bedroom faced the lane. From the road, you couldn't see me. Just the light behind the curtain. And suddenly all those questions sounded different.
I took the phone to my mum. I tried to start with the first message, but I couldn't get the words out. So I just handed it over.
She read it twice. Then she shut the curtain. That tiny thing, the sound of those rings sliding across the rail, is what I remember most.
The next morning she came to school with me. We took screenshots. My friend told them about the shop. For once, I didn't have to make it sound harmless.
He called it concern. Said I'd taken it the wrong way. Mum asked why concern needed to be a secret. He didn't answer that.
I was moved to another class while the school dealt with it. Mum collected me for a while. The messages stopped. I wasn't told everything that happened after that.
For weeks, even with my phone switched off, I'd look at it when a car slowed outside. I used to check the curtain before I checked my homework.
And that first line? The one about my bedroom light? He said it when Mum was standing right there. I was only checking you were getting enough sleep.
He sounded so reasonable. That's the part that still bothers me. He said it like we'd misunderstood him. Like watching my window was the most normal thing in the world.
